bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
bib.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly integrated in user-facing technology, but public understanding of these technologies is often limited. There is a need for additional HCI research investigating a) what competencies users need in order to effectively interact with and critically evaluate AI and b) how to design learner-centered AI technologies that foster increased user understanding of AI. This paper takes a step towards realizing both of these goals by providing a concrete definition of AI literacy based on existing research. We synthesize a variety of interdisciplinary literature into a set of core competencies of AI literacy and suggest several design considerations to support AI developers and educators in creating learner-centered AI. These competencies and design considerations are organized in a conceptual framework thematically derived from the literature. This paper's contributions can be used to start a conversation about and guide future research on AI literacy within the HCI community.
bib.title: What is AI Literacy? Competencies and Design Considerations

bib.abstract: Personality assessments provide insights into understanding individual differences. In HCI, personality assessments are used to model user behavior or tailor user interfaces. However, conventional Likert-scale personality tests face issues in user engagement and capturing comprehensive personality nuances. Building upon prior work using conversational user interfaces for personality prediction, we delve deeper into personalized personality tests. Through a formative study (n=4), we identified three design goals for user engagement. Informed by these goals, we propose a novel architecture integrating multiple large language model agents to support free-form conversation-based personality assessment. Our system, ChatFive, predicts users’ Big Five traits through real-time personalized dialogue. Evaluations from our user study (n=20) revealed that ChatFive significantly improved conveying true responses and felt more engaged, though requiring longer response times and different validation. We discuss the limitations on the validity of ChatFive and its implications.
bib.title: ChatFive: Enhancing User Experience in Likert Scale Personality Test through Interactive Conversation with LLM Agents

bib.abstract: We present Skinput, a technology that appropriates the human body for acoustic transmission, allowing the skin to be used as an input surface. In particular, we resolve the location of finger taps on the arm and hand by analyzing mechanical vibrations that propagate through the body. We collect these signals using a novel array of sensors worn as an armband. This approach provides an always available, naturally portable, and on-body finger input system. We assess the capabilities, accuracy and limitations of our technique through a two-part, twenty-participant user study. To further illustrate the utility of our approach, we conclude with several proof-of-concept applications we developed.

bib.abstract: In this work, we analyze the different contexts in which one chooses to integrate artificial intelligence into an interface and the implications of this choice in managing user interaction. While AI in systems can provide significant benefits, it is not infallible and can make errors that seriously affect users. We aim to understand how to design more robust human-AI systems so that these initial AI errors do not lead to more catastrophic failures. To prevent failures, it is essential to detect errors as early as possible and have clear mechanisms to repair them. However, detecting errors in AI systems can be challenging. Therefore, we examine various approaches to error detection and repair, including post-hoc estimation, the use of traces and ambiguity, and multiple sensor layers.

bib.abstract: Over the last decade, there has been an explosion of work around social media within CSCW. A range of perspectives have been applied to the use of social media, which we characterise as aggregate, actor-focussed or a combination. We outline the opportunities for a perspective informed by ethnomethodology and conversation analysis (EMCA)-an orientation that has been influential within CSCW, yet has only rarely been applied to social media use. EMCA approaches can complement existing perspectives through articulating how social media is embedded in the everyday lives of its users and how sequentiality of social media use organises this embeddedness. We draw on a corpus of screen and ambient audio recordings of mobile device use to show how EMCA research is generative for understanding social media through concepts such as adjacency pairs, sequential context, turn allocation / speaker selection, and repair.
bib.title: Embeddedness and sequentiality in social media

bib.abstract: We present the notion of "bridging concepts" as a particular form of intermediary knowledge in HCI research, residing between theory and practice. We argue that bridging concepts address the challenge of facilitating exchange between theory and practice in HCI, and we compare it to other intermediary forms of knowledge such as strong concepts and conceptual constructs. We propose that bridging concepts have three defining constituents: a theoretical foundation, a set of design articulations and a range of exemplars that demonstrate the scope and potential of their application. These constituents specify how bridging concepts, as a form of knowledge, are accountable to both theory and practice. We present an analysis of the concept of "peepholes" as an example of a bridging concept aimed at spurring user curiosity and engagement.

bib.abstract: Over the last 10 years, Computer-Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) has identified a base set of findings. These findings are taken almost as assumptions within the field. In summary, they argue that human activity is highly flexible, nuanced, and contextualized and that computational entities such as information sharing, roles, and social norms need to be similarly flexible, nuanced, and contextualized. However, current systems cannot fully support the social world uncovered by these findings. In this article I argue that there is an inherent gap between the social requirements of CSCW and its technical mechanisms. The social-technical gap is the divide between what we know we must support socially and what we can support technically. Exploring, understanding, and hopefully ameliorating this social-technical gap is the central challenge for CSCW as a field and one of the central problems for human-computer interaction. Indeed, merely attesting the continued centrality of this gap could be one of the important intellectual contributions of CSCW. I also argue that the challenge of the social-technical gap creates an opportunity to refocus CSCW.
bib.title: The intellectual challenge of CSCW: the gap between social requirements and technical feasibility

bib.abstract: Prior studies have shown that gratifications exert significant effects on the sustained use of an information system by individuals. However, the roles of different gratifications vary in predicting continuance usage in different research contexts. Also, less attention has been paid to how gratifications affect the continuance intention to use WeChat. The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of different gratifications on the continuance intention to use WeChat in China. Based on the uses and gratifications theory, a theoretical model is developed, which identifies four types of gratification: hedonic gratification, social gratification, utilitarian gratification and technology gratification. Data were collected via a questionnaire survey from 297 WeChat users in China, and further analyzed using PLS-SEM. The results show that, technology gratification (media appeal) has the greatest effect on the continuance intention to use WeChat, followed by hedonic gratification (perceived enjoyment) and utilitarian gratification (information sharing). This study examines the effects of gratifications on continuance intention.Technology gratification affects WeChat users' continuance intention strongly.Hedonic gratification affects WeChat users' continuance intention.Utilitarian gratification affects WeChat users' continuance intention.Social gratification exerts no effect on WeChat users' continuance intention.
bib.title: Understanding the effects of gratifications on the continuance intention to use WeChat in China

bib.keywords: Dependency, Human-Centred AI, Responsible AI
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Human-Agent Interaction
bib.abstract: The role of intelligent agents in research on AI is becoming increasingly significant. The study of embodied intelligent systems, such as social and companion robots, is growing steadily in proportion to the previsions that they will become increasingly involved in the everyday lives of individuals. Non-embodied intelligent systems, such as chatbots or virtual voice assistants, are already part of many people’s everyday experience, being constantly at their disposal. This necessitates a re-evaluation of society as we know it, which must be conceived as a ‘hybrid society’. The objective of this paper is to demonstrate how, in such a scenario, a truly human-centred development of intelligent agents necessitates a design that does not capitalise or exploit the natural inclination towards human attachment and empathy, but rather incorporates this into a more responsible framework for human-agent interaction (henceforth HAI). In order to achieve this objective, the topic of human dependency is presented, analysed, and interpreted in the light of one of its main theorisation, formulated in the socio-legal domain. The merit of such a theoretical framework is that it is flexible enough to be applied to all those elements that, once introduced into society, can affect it and alter its equilibrium. This is undoubtedly the case with the artificial agents designated for HAI. Building on this, the paper demonstrates how such an approach could be employed to analyse the dynamics of HAI in a truly human-centred manner, thereby providing a foundation for the future design of artificial agents and the dynamics of interaction with end-users.
bib.title: Human-Agent Interaction and Human Dependency: Possible New Approaches for Old Challenges

bib.keywords: ChatGPT, higher education, novelty value, perceived humanness, personality
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on Advances in Information Technology
bib.abstract: The emergence of ChatGPT as a generative AI tool has revolutionized the educational scenario by bringing in unprecedented changes. In this respect exploring the factors that affect the adoption and acceptance of ChatGPT services for educational purpose is of utmost importance. Accordingly, in this work we take a hybrid psycho-technical approach by considering the technological (perceived usefulness, ease of use and facilitating conditions), contextual (perceived humanness and novelty value), and psychological (agreeableness, extraversion, openness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism) gratifications of ChatGPT use. Data is collected from a sample of university students who use ChatGPT regularly across two Asian countries. The data analysis is done using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling. Results indicate that among the technical factors only perceived usefulness successfully predicts ChatGPT usage. Both the contextual factors of humanness and novelty use significantly explain ChatGPT usage. Finally, among the psychological factors’ openness, agreeableness, and neuroticism determine the usage scenario, however, the later two are found to be negatively associated with ChatGPT usage.
bib.title: University Students’ Acceptance and Usage of Generative AI (ChatGPT) from a Psycho-Technical Perspective

bib.abstract: While Interactive systems such as Chatbots, are well known in personal environments with technologies like “Apple’s Siri” or the “Google’s Assistant”, the acceptance of said technologies in the enterprise context has hardly been examined. Literature shows that these technologies hold great potential for enterprises as they can increase productivity and are cost-efficient by automating processes. Still, to not alienate employees when introducing these systems called Enterprise Bots in this paper, it is crucial to understand how employees accept and adopt these new systems. This paper derives a research model based on the decomposed Theory of Planned Behaviour, which is tested in a survey with 198 participants. Results from a structural equation model show that intrinsic motivation of the employees has a strong positive influence on the intention to use Enterprise Bots whereas external influences showed smaller effects. The results indicate that it is important that employees are convinced of the usefulness of a tool for themselves. The paper provides theoretical insights and helps decision makers to introduce such systems.

bib.abstract: This study provides nascent information on university students' needs to adopt social networking sites (SNSs) pervasively. The study drew from the uses and gratifications theory (UGT) and social influence (SI) processes framework. Relevant hypotheses were formulated to test the proposed research model. Data was collected in a survey of university undergraduates in four countries in the Americas (i.e., United States, Canada, Mexico, and Argentina). Data analysis using partial least squares (PLS) supported 8 out of the 10 hypotheses formulated. The SI process of internalization and identification, as well as UGT categories of self-discovery, entertainment value, social enhancement, and the need to maintain interpersonal connectivity through the construct of behavioral intentions, were found to have positive impacts on students' pervasive adoption of SNSs. The results also revealed that the cultural factor of individualism–collectivism had a positive impact on the pervasive adoption of SNSs, such that greater levels of engagement were observed for students from more individualistic cultures.

bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 5th International Conference on Conversational User Interfaces
bib.abstract: Research on voice assistants has primarily studied how people use them for informational needs, music requests, and to control electronic devices (e.g., IoT). Recent research suggests people such as older adults want to use them to address social and relational needs, but lacks empirical evidence to show how older adults are currently engaging in these behaviors. In this paper, we use a machine learning approach to analyze more than 600,000 queries that 456 older adults in assisted living communities made to Amazon Alexa devices over two years, classifying how older adults use voice assistants for social well-being purposes. We present empirical evidence showing how older adults engage in three primary relational behaviors with Alexa – 1) asking personal questions to "get to know" the assistant, 2) asking for advice and 3) engaging with the voice assistant to alleviate stress. We use these findings to discuss ethical implications of voice assistant use in long-term care settings.

bib.keywords: AI assistants, alignment, ethics, governance, philosophy, sociotechnical systems, trust, trustworthy
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 2024 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency
bib.abstract: As AI assistants become increasingly sophisticated and deeply integrated into our lives, questions of trust rise to the forefront. In this paper, we build on philosophical studies of trust to investigate when user trust in AI assistants is justified. By moving beyond a focus on the technical artefact in isolation, we consider the broader societal system in which AI assistants are developed and deployed. We conceptualise user trust in AI assistants as encompassing two main targets, namely AI assistants and their developers. We argue that – as AI assistants become more human like and exhibit increased agency – discerning when user trust is justified requires consideration not only of competence, on the part of AI assistants and their developers, but also alignment between the competing interests, values or incentives of AI assistants, developers and users. To help users understand if and when their trust in the competence and alignment of AI assistants and developers is justified, we propose a sociotechnical approach that requires evidence to be collected at three levels: AI assistant design, organisational practices and third-party governance. Taken together, these measures can help harness the transformative potential of AI assistants while also ensuring their operation is ethical and value aligned.
bib.title: Should Users Trust Advanced AI Assistants? Justified Trust As a Function of Competence and Alignment

bib.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integral to educational systems, understanding policy guidelines and recommendations from various sources is crucial. This meta-synthesis examines AI policies and guidelines from peer-reviewed articles, reports, books, and websites from 2020 to 2024, with a focus on their implications for teaching and learning. Using a thematic analysis approach, the study categorizes findings into key themes and subthemes. Under the theme of policies and guidelines, notable subthemes include ethical AI use, AI literacy, and inclusivity and equity. In terms of implementation strategies, the synthesis identifies crucial areas such as student orientation and professional development, enhanced teaching tools and data-driven insights, improved student learning outcomes and engagement, and streamlined administrative processes. The study also determines practical constraints that challenge the successful integration of AI in education, including technical and integration challenges, training and support issues, ethical and fairness concerns, cost and accessibility, transparency and privacy issues, and misalignment with educational goals. Future research may explore the long-term impacts of AI integration policies and guidelines, refine practical implementation strategies, and foster collaboration among researchers, educators, and policymakers to tackle ongoing challenges and maximize AI's potential in education.
bib.keywords: AI ethics, AI integration, AI in education, AI in teaching and learning, Artificial intelligence, ChatGPT

bib.keywords: appropriate trust, complementary performance, distribution shift, human-AI decision making, interactive explanations
bib.abstract: Although AI holds promise for improving human decision making in societally critical domains, it remains an open question how human-AI teams can reliably outperform AI alone and human alone in challenging prediction tasks (also known as complementary performance). We explore two directions to understand the gaps in achieving complementary performance. First, we argue that the typical experimental setup limits the potential of human-AI teams. To account for lower AI performance out-of-distribution than in-distribution because of distribution shift, we design experiments with different distribution types and investigate human performance for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution examples. Second, we develop novel interfaces to support interactive explanations so that humans can actively engage with AI assistance. Using virtual pilot studies and large-scale randomized experiments across three tasks, we demonstrate a clear difference between in-distribution and out-of-distribution, and observe mixed results for interactive explanations: while interactive explanations improve human perception of AI assistance's usefulness, they may reinforce human biases and lead to limited performance improvement. Overall, our work points out critical challenges and future directions towards enhancing human performance with AI assistance.
bib.title: Understanding the Effect of Out-of-distribution Examples and Interactive Explanations on Human-AI Decision Making
bib.author: Liu, Han and Lai, Vivian and Tan, Chenhao

bib.keywords: artificial intelligence, explainability, human-grounded evaluations, interactivity, interpretability
bib.booktitle: Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
bib.abstract: Explainability (XAI) has matured in recent years to provide more human-centered explanations of AI-based decision systems. While static explanations remain predominant, interactive XAI has gathered momentum to support the human cognitive process of explaining. However, the evidence regarding the benefits of interactive explanations is unclear. In this paper, we map existing findings by conducting a detailed scoping review of 48 empirical studies in which interactive explanations are evaluated with human users. We also create a classification of interactive techniques specific to XAI and group the resulting categories according to their role in the cognitive process of explanation: "selective", "mutable" or "dialogic". We identify the effects of interactivity on several user-based metrics. We find that interactive explanations improve perceived usefulness and performance of the human+AI team but take longer. We highlight conflicting results regarding cognitive load and overconfidence. Lastly, we describe underexplored areas including measuring curiosity or learning or perturbing outcomes.
bib.title: On Selective, Mutable and Dialogic XAI: a Review of What Users Say about Different Types of Interactive Explanations

bib.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in daily decision-making processes, the need for effective communication between humans and AI systems grows more crucial. The Adaptive XAI (AXAI) workshop, now in its second edition, focuses on developing intelligent interfaces that can adaptively explain AI’s decision-making processes. Building on the success of our inaugural event at IUI 2024, this workshop continues to explore the intersection of Explainable AI and adaptive user interfaces, emphasizing the development of interfaces that dynamically adapt to create explanations that resonate with diverse users. In line with the human-centric principles of the Future Artificial Intelligence Research (FAIR) project, we examine how emerging technologies such as conversational agents and Large Language Models can enhance AI explainability while ensuring explanations remain malleable and responsive to users’ evolving cognitive states and contextual needs.
bib.title: Adaptive XAI: Advancing Intelligent Interfaces for Tailored AI Explanations (2nd Edition)

bib.abstract: AI systems are increasingly being adopted across various domains and application areas. With this surge, there is a growing research focus and societal concern for actively involving humans in developing, operating, and adopting these systems. Despite this concern, most existing literature on AI and Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) primarily focuses on explaining how AI systems operate and, at times, allowing users to contest AI decisions. Existing studies often overlook more impactful forms of user interaction with AI systems, such as giving users agency beyond contestability and enabling them to adapt and even co-design the AI’s internal mechanics. In this survey, we aim to bridge this gap by reviewing the state-of-the-art in Human-Centered AI literature, the domain where AI and HCI studies converge, extending past Explainable and Contestable AI, delving into the Interactive AI and beyond. Our analysis contributes to shaping the trajectory of future Interactive AI design and advocates for a more user-centric approach that provides users with greater agency, fostering not only their understanding of AI’s workings but also their active engagement in its development and evolution.

bib.abstract: The proposed EU regulation for Artificial Intelligence (AI), the AI Act, has sparked some debate about the role of explainable AI (XAI) in high-risk AI systems. Some argue that black-box AI models will have to be replaced with transparent ones, others argue that using XAI techniques might help in achieving compliance. This work aims to bring some clarity as regards XAI in the context of the AI Act and focuses in particular on the AI Act requirements for transparency and human oversight. After outlining key points of the debate and describing the current limitations of XAI techniques, this paper carries out an interdisciplinary analysis of how the AI Act addresses the issue of opaque AI systems. In particular, we argue that neither does the AI Act mandate a requirement for XAI, which is the subject of intense scientific research and is not without technical limitations, nor does it ban the use of black-box AI systems. Instead, the AI Act aims to achieve its stated policy objectives with the focus on transparency (including documentation) and human oversight. Finally, in order to concretely illustrate our findings and conclusions, a use case on AI-based proctoring is presented.
bib.title: The role of explainable AI in the context of the AI Act
bib.author: Panigutti, Cecilia and Hamon, Ronan and Hupont, Isabelle and Fernandez Llorca, David and Fano Yela, Delia and Junklewitz, Henrik and Scalzo, Salvatore and Mazzini, Gabriele and Sanchez, Ignacio and Soler Garrido, Josep and Gomez, Emilia

bib.abstract: With the rise of artificial intelligence (AI), concerns about AI applications causing unforeseen harms to safety, privacy, security, and fairness are intensifying. While attempts to create regulations are underway, with initiatives such as the EU AI Act and the 2023 White House executive order, skepticism abounds as to the efficacy of such regulations. This paper explores an interdisciplinary approach to designing policy for the explainability of AI applications, as the widely discussed "right to explanation" associated with the EU General Data Protection Regulation is ambiguous. To develop practical guidance for explainability, we conducted an experimental study that involved continuous collaboration among a team of researchers with AI and policy backgrounds over the course of ten weeks. The objective was to determine whether, through interdisciplinary effort, we can reach consensus on a policy for explainability in AI–one that is clearer, and more actionable and enforceable than current guidelines. We share nine observations, derived from an iterative policy design process, which included drafting the policy, attempting to comply with it (or circumvent it), and collectively evaluating its effectiveness on a weekly basis. Key observations include: iterative and continuous feedback was useful to improve policy drafts over time, discussing evidence of compliance was necessary during policy design, and human-subject studies were found to be an important form of evidence. We conclude with a note of optimism, arguing that meaningful policies can be achieved within a moderate time frame and with limited experience in policy design, as demonstrated by our student researchers on the team. This holds promising implications for policymakers, signaling that practical and effective regulation for AI applications is attainable.
bib.title: Regulating Explainability in Machine Learning Applications -- Observations from a Policy Design Experiment

bib.abstract:
Objective
Despite rising popularity and performance, studies evaluating the use of large language models for clinical decision support are lacking. Here, we evaluate ChatGPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer)-3.5 and GPT-4’s (OpenAI, San Francisco, California) capacity for clinical decision support in radiology via the identification of appropriate imaging services for two important clinical presentations: breast cancer screening and breast pain.
Methods
We compared ChatGPT’s responses to the ACR Appropriateness Criteria for breast pain and breast cancer screening. Our prompt formats included an open-ended (OE) and a select all that apply (SATA) format. Scoring criteria evaluated whether proposed imaging modalities were in accordance with ACR guidelines. Three replicate entries were conducted for each prompt, and the average of these was used to determine final scores.
Results
Both ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4 achieved an average OE score of 1.830 (out of 2) for breast cancer screening prompts. ChatGPT-3.5 achieved a SATA average percentage correct of 88.9%, compared with ChatGPT-4’s average percentage correct of 98.4% for breast cancer screening prompts. For breast pain, ChatGPT-3.5 achieved an average OE score of 1.125 (out of 2) and a SATA average percentage correct of 58.3%, as compared with an average OE score of 1.666 (out of 2) and a SATA average percentage correct of 77.7%.
Discussion
Our results demonstrate the eventual feasibility of using large language models like ChatGPT for radiologic decision making, with the potential to improve clinical workflow and responsible use of radiology services. More use cases and greater accuracy are necessary to evaluate and implement such tools.
bib.keywords: AI, breast imaging, ChatGPT, clinical decision making, clinical decision support
bib.author: Arya Rao and John Kim and Meghana Kamineni and Michael Pang and Winston Lie and Keith J. Dreyer and Marc D. Succi
bib.journal: Journal of the American College of Radiology
bib.title: Evaluating GPT as an Adjunct for Radiologic Decision Making: GPT-4 Versus GPT-3.5 in a Breast Imaging Pilot

bib.abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning have been transforming the landscape of scientific research. Out of which, the chatbot technology has experienced tremendous advancements in recent years, especially with ChatGPT emerging as a notable AI language model. This comprehensive review delves into the background, applications, key challenges, and future directions of ChatGPT. We begin by exploring its origins, development, and underlying technology, before examining its wide-ranging applications across industries such as customer service, healthcare, and education. We also highlight the critical challenges that ChatGPT faces, including ethical concerns, data biases, and safety issues, while discussing potential mitigation strategies. Finally, we envision the future of ChatGPT by exploring areas of further research and development, focusing on its integration with other technologies, improved human-AI interaction, and addressing the digital divide. This review offers valuable insights for researchers, developers, and stakeholders interested in the ever-evolving landscape of AI-driven conversational agents. This study explores the various ways ChatGPT has been revolutionizing scientific research, spanning from data processing and hypothesis generation to collaboration and public outreach. Furthermore, the paper examines the potential challenges and ethical concerns surrounding the use of ChatGPT in research, while highlighting the importance of striking a balance between AI-assisted innovation and human expertise. The paper presents several ethical issues in existing computing domain and how ChatGPT can invoke challenges to such notion. This work also includes some biases and limitations of ChatGPT. It is worth to note that despite of several controversies and ethical concerns, ChatGPT has attracted remarkable attentions from academia, research, and industries in a very short span of time.
bib.keywords: ChatGPT, Language model, GPT-3.5, Generative AI, Conversational AI, Context understanding, Natural language processing
bib.author: Partha Pratim Ray
bib.journal: Internet of Things and Cyber-Physical Systems
bib.title: ChatGPT: A comprehensive review on background, applications, key challenges, bias, ethics, limitations and future scope

bib.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with chat-based capabilities, such as ChatGPT, are widely used in various workflows. However, due to a limited understanding of these large-scale models, users struggle to use this technology and experience different kinds of dissatisfaction. Researchers have introduced several methods, such as prompt engineering, to improve model responses. However, they focus on enhancing the model’s performance in specific tasks, and little has been investigated on how to deal with the user dissatisfaction resulting from the model’s responses. Therefore, with ChatGPT as the case study, we examine users’ dissatisfaction along with their strategies to address the dissatisfaction. After organizing users’ dissatisfaction with LLM into seven categories based on a literature review, we collected 511 instances of dissatisfactory ChatGPT responses from 107 users and their detailed recollections of dissatisfactory experiences, which we released as a publicly accessible dataset. Our analysis reveals that users most frequently experience dissatisfaction when ChatGPT fails to grasp their intentions, while they rate the severity of dissatisfaction related to accuracy the highest. We also identified four tactics users employ to address their dissatisfaction and their effectiveness. We found that users often do not use any tactics to address their dissatisfaction, and even when using tactics, 72\% of dissatisfaction remained unresolved. Moreover, we found that users with low knowledge of LLMs tend to face more dissatisfaction on accuracy while they often put minimal effort in addressing dissatisfaction. Based on these findings, we propose design implications for minimizing user dissatisfaction and enhancing the usability of chat-based LLM.
bib.title: Understanding Users’ Dissatisfaction with ChatGPT Responses: Types, Resolving Tactics, and the Effect of Knowledge Level

\section{Introduction}

The allure of artificial intelligence (AI) has captivated the public imagination, promising a future where intelligent machines seamlessly integrate into our lives, anticipating our needs, and effortlessly completing tasks. Upon first glance, the vision of ubiquitous computing presented by Mark Wieser,  a future where technology seamlessly blends into the background of our lives, is here in a way we have not experienced before \cite{Weisermagic}. However, Wieser also cautioned against the allure of "magic," where the inner workings of technology become opaque and user understanding fades into mere acceptance \cite{Weisermagic}. The current wave of AI personal assistants, with their sleek designs and promises of effortless efficiency, embodies this tension between integration and transparency. The promise is particularly potent in the realm of personal assistants, where devices like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin are fueled by compelling marketing campaigns, have emerged as harbingers of this AI-powered future. 

In a YouTube video that had more than four million views (see Figure \ref{fig:YT_review}) reviewing one AI-powered personal assistant product - Rabbit R1, the video producer, 
`Coffeezilla', refers to the device as a scam because it does not actually accomplish promised features that would allow the device to know the details of one's daily routine and help them while accomplishing those tasks. Promotional claims for Rabbit R1 directly quoted in the YouTube video included the ability to  \textit{``speak or type with [Rabbit] R1. I can also use R1 to call a ride I can also use R1 to order food I can also make R1 perform a set of more complex actions. For example, if I want to plan a trip, I can just describe what I want in full.''} The YouTube influencer then details his negative experiences with the product, saying that it does not perform any of these advertised tasks. Specifically, he tries to order an Uber, and the R1 device stated \textit{``ride share status is currently unavailable...apologies the Uber ride request could not be processed.''} The conclusion of the product review ultimately points to the failure of the central AI functionality of the Rabbit R1 called a Large Action Model \cite{zitron_rabbit_2024}. The LAM is supposed to learn the actions that users want to do as well as bypassing different APIs to take action on platforms like Uber, Spotify, and DoorDash\cite{shepherd_lam_2024}. The reviews argue that the LAM cannot learn from user actions, nor can it bridge digital platform ecosystems \cite{van2018platform}. Although many responses expressed deep confusion about how the tasks marketed for the device differed from those already available through existing technologies, such as cell phones or voice assistants like Amazon Alexa, there was also notable interest in the "artificial intelligence" component of the device. 

\begin{figure}[h!]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.80\linewidth]{YT_review.png}
    \caption{A video questioning whether the Rabbit R1 was a scam as a product}
    \label{fig:YT_review}
\end{figure}

As AI personal assistants proliferate, understanding their real-world usage and value becomes paramount. Observing how people integrate devices like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin, alongside subscription services like Ohai.ai and Docus AI, reveals not only the practical benefits but also the discrepancies between marketing promises and lived experiences. Our study delves into this rapidly evolving landscape, examining the persistent gap between the aspirational claims of these technologies and their actual day-to-day use.

We build on Ackerman’s notion of the sociotechnical gap—the disconnect between what is socially desirable and what is technically feasible—and analyze how this divide manifests as uncertainties in AI personal assistants \cite{AckermanGap}. Drawing on Uses and Gratifications Theory \cite{katz1973uses,wei2024gratification}, we examine how users adopt these systems to fulfill four distinct needs: technological, utilitarian, hedonic, and social gratification. Simultaneously, we incorporate Uncertainty Reduction Theory \cite{zhang2022uncertainty,kramer1999motivation} to explain how uncertainties surrounding system functionality, interaction, and social role disrupt those gratifications.

Specifically, we introduce three categories of uncertainty: functional, interactional, and social. Each of these maps onto one or more user gratifications and offer a lens for understanding user frustrations and eventual adaptations. We then offer design recommendations aimed at closing the sociotechnical gap and building more transparent and context-aware AI systems.

\section{Related Work}
This section examines the evolving landscape of AI-powered conversational assistants, tracing their technological development, user motivations, and design implications. In \S\ref{sec:CA}, we begin by highlighting the shift from early text-based tools like Clippy to today’s large language model-powered assistants, and showing how these systems have become integrated into everyday routines and domestic settings. We then turn to two theoretical lenses to interpret adoption and usage: Uses and Gratifications Theory (\S\ref{UGT}) identifies four types of user motivations—technological, hedonic, utilitarian, and social—that shape how people engage with AI assistants, while Uncertainty Reduction Theory (\S\ref{URT}) explains how users manage uncertainty when adopting new AI systems. In \S\ref{humanai_design}, we explore emerging design challenges around user autonomy, system transparency, and the role of embodiment in AI design. Finally, \S\ref{sub:multi-device} expands the scope to emphasize that conversational assistants are rarely used in isolation. Instead, they operate within broader constellations of tools and services that require thoughtful integration to support user control and collaboration.

\subsection{Evolution of Conversational Assistants}
\label{sec:CA}
A foundational example of a digital assistant was Microsoft’s Clippy, which demonstrated the potential of text-based natural language feedback despite its unpopularity \cite{mutchler2018timeline, baym2019intelligent}. It offered early insights into virtual assistant design, including the importance of responding only when summoned \cite{Satyanarayanan}. More advanced “legacy assistants” like Siri (launched in 2011), Alexa (launched in 2014), and Google Assistant (launched in 2016) introduced voice interactions for tasks such as setting reminders and controlling smart home devices. Analyses of Google Home usage show that these assistants are primarily used for music, hands-free search, and IoT automation \cite{ammari_et_al_19, zhang2018understanding}, including integration with devices such as smart lights (e.g., Philips Hue \cite{philips_hue}), thermostats (e.g., Nest \cite{nest_thermostat}), stereo systems (e.g., Sonos \cite{sonos}), and cameras (e.g., Nest Cam \cite{nest_cam}). These assistants became embedded into household routines through automation rules and were shaped by the complexity of domestic environments \cite{porcheron_voice_2018, rode_domestic_2005, tolmie_digital_2010}. Voice interaction, as a natural modality, simulates human dialogue to complete tasks \cite{nass_can_1995}, with task completion influencing user satisfaction \cite{shechtman_media_2003, kiseleva_understanding_2016}. The newest generation of AI assistants, powered by large language models like GPT and Claude, leverages NLP and machine learning to deliver more integrated and versatile user experiences \cite{roslan2023rise}.

However, when assistants fail to complete tasks, users engage in repair strategies. Group-based interactions with Siri show users treating it as a humanlike agent \cite{porcheron_animals_2017, luger_like_2016}. Amazon reviews reveal emotional attachments to Alexa, framing it as a companion \cite{purington_alexa_2017}. These assistants now play social as well as functional roles, raising design challenges around agency, privacy, and user expectations.

\subsubsection{Uses and Gratifications Theory} \label{UGT}
The Uses and Gratifications Theory (UGT) offers a user-centered perspective on technology adoption by emphasizing the personal needs and motivations that drive engagement \cite{katz1973uses, rubin2009uses, lin2024unraveling}. It distinguishes between anticipated and actual gratifications experienced through technology use \cite{mclean2019hey}. UGT has been widely applied to media and technology studies \cite{wei2024gratification}, including research on AI technologies such as chatbots and smart assistants \cite{xie2023understanding}. In the context of voice assistants like Amazon Alexa, studies show that both utilitarian (e.g., efficiency) and symbolic (e.g., identity and status) benefits shape adoption \cite{ammari_et_al_19, mclean2019hey, yadav2024understanding}. These insights have led to the identification of four key gratification types that guide user interaction with AI systems \cite{Ganunderstanding}.

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Technological Gratification}: satisfaction derived from engaging with advanced or novel technologies. For example, McLean et al. \cite{mclean2019hey} echo earlier studies about the early adoption of voice assistants like Amazon Alexa \cite{ammari_et_al_19} and showing that users might adopt these technologies to enhance their image and social status, much like people purchase luxury items for status.
    \item \textbf{Hedonic Gratifiction}: pleasure-driven gratification where the enjoyment users gain from using the technology or a specific use-case of the technology. For example, users who find pleasure in engaging with voice assistants for tasks like playing music or casual conversations \cite{ammari_et_al_19} would have a stronger intention to use them in the future \cite{jo2022continuance} and a player who enjoys the immersive and elements of a game is more likely to continue playing due to the pleasurable experiences it offers \cite{li2015modeling}.
    \item \textbf{Utilitarian Gratification}: practical benefits of a technology use such as efficiency in everyday routines \cite{ammari_et_al_19}, and accomplishing daily tasks. For example, Brachten et al. \cite{BRACHTEN2021102375} describe how employees in an organization appreciated chatbots that could efficiently handle routine inquiries, thereby allowing them to focus on more complex tasks.
    \item \textbf{Social Gratification}: the satisfaction individuals obtain from using media or technology to fulfill their social needs, such as connecting with others, building relationships, and enhancing social interactions \cite{xie2023understanding}. For example, students experience social gratification by engaging with SNSs to stay connected with peers and expand their social networks \cite{IFINEDO2016192}.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Uncertainty Reduction Theory} \label{URT}
Users have specific ways of coping and maintaining their uncertainties in their experiences with the use or presence of AI. Chang et al. introduced two key uncertainty reduction strategies for generative AI systems like ChatGPT: ``interactive" uncertainty reduction strategies, which involves direct engagement with the system or other users, and ``passive" uncertainty reduction strategies which involves users reducing uncertainty by observing others’ interactions with the AI systems \cite{chang2024uncertainty}. 

Consistent with earlier findings on AI adoption, we found Uncertainty Reduction Theory useful for understanding how users seek to reduce uncertainty in their decision-making processes when adopting new technologies \cite{kramer1999motivation}. Combining UGT and URT provides a robust framework for understanding technology use and adoption \cite{chang2024uncertainty}. We further examine this interplay between uncertainties and gratifications in our subsequent sections.

\subsection{From Affordances to Experience: Design Challenges in Human-AI Interaction}  \label{humanai_design}
As conversational agents become more intelligent by incorporating AI, emerging design challenges must be addressed to ensure their usability. A recurring issue is the gap in understanding AI capabilities—designers often struggle to grasp what AI can and cannot do \cite{Dove,11qianyang,wangzimmermann}, a problem compounded by the general public’s limited knowledge of machine learning. Bridging technical affordances (such as conversational interaction or multi-modal feedback) \cite{10Lars,12Qian} with user experience requires rethinking how AI systems are designed and deployed \cite{luger_like_2016,kuniavsky2017designing,lancaster}.

Some examples of these gaps include AI assistants' frequent misinterpretation of user intent, where the system overlooks contextual cues or fails to infer goals accurately, resulting in outputs that do not align with user expectations \cite{RAO2023990, kim_et_al_24}. This misalignment can be made worse if users also see the tone of the response as out of step with their expectations (e.g., formal or flat tone) \cite{RAY2023121}. Finally, the system sometimes refuses to engage with controversial or sensitive topics—especially when paired with generic disclaimers that do not provide explanations for refusal— which can also be perceived as unhelpful or obstructive \cite{borji2023categorical}. 

Foundational HCI principles, as proposed by Shneiderman and others, remain central to AI design \cite{textshneiderman2010designing, Shneidermanpaperarticle, ShneidermanPattie,MacKenzietextbook2024,6NorthChris}. Core features such as intuitive search, direct manipulation \cite{Buschek}, and immediate visual feedback continue to guide good design \cite{leeminha, 6NorthChris}. User autonomy is especially critical \cite{Dove}, aligning with long-standing debates between user-controlled systems and agent-based automation \cite{Nass, 3beun2003embodied,luger_like_2016}. Yet, intelligent systems often lead to unrealistic user expectations, particularly in complex or sensitive contexts \cite{Cranshaw,reexamining,zhangjoy}. When users lack control or struggle to understand system behavior, frustration and abandonment may result \cite{Bisante,zhanjoydc}. Educating users about a system’s limitations can align expectations and improve satisfaction \cite{stone2022artificial, hinderks2019developing}.

Embodiment also plays a critical role in AI design. While human-like agents can support social interaction, excessive anthropomorphism can mislead users \cite{dautenhahn2007socially}. Research emphasizes that embodiment should focus on functional and social cues, not mimicry \cite{DeAngeli,3beun2003embodied,Nass}. Designing effective embodied agents requires understanding both conversational roles and how users adapt within broader sociotechnical contexts, thereby prioritizing design approaches that center on user experience \cite{hinderks2019developing}.

\subsection{Considering Multi-Device Ecosystems} \label{sub:multi-device}
The success or failure of new technologies often depends on how well they integrate into users' existing ecosystems. Forlizzi’s concept of product ecologies highlights that a product’s meaning and value emerge from a dynamic network of relationships—among users, technologies, social contexts, and environments—rather than from functional features alone \cite{forlizzi2008product, suchman1987plans, suchman2007human}. This approach emphasizes the interconnected nature of these factors, showing how changes in one part of the ecology can impact user behavior, technology adoption, and future design directions.

Extending this framework, Rossitto et al. examined how teamwork is supported through constellations of tools distributed across people and spaces \cite{rossitto2014understanding}. They found that such configurations are unique to each group and shaped by shared values, routines, and work divisions. Ignoring these multi-device interactions risks creating niche technologies with limited interoperability, reducing fluid collaboration \cite{rossitto2014understanding}. While personal assistants appear tailored to individual use, they exist within broader ecosystems of devices and services that shift with context and task. As such, seamless integration and communication across platforms are critical to supporting user agency and control.

\section{Context and Methods}
The first wave of AI devices, including the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1, arrived on the consumer market in early 2024. The Humane AI Pin, after much anticipation, officially launched on November 9, 2023, with pre-orders opening that same week.  The Rabbit R1, while lacking the same pre-launch fanfare, also hit the market in early 2024. At the same time subscription-based AI services like Ohai.ai and Docus AI began carving out their niches. Ohai debuted in mid-2023, while Docus followed suit in early 2024. These services, unlike their device counterparts, are powered by generative AI models like OpenAI's GPT, suggesting a potential technological divide for how artificial intelligence is used between wearables and subscription services. 
Devices like the Humane AI Pin and the Rabbit R1 represent the tangible manifestation of AI assistants, offering hands-free interaction through voice commands and even gestures in the case of the Humane Pin. These devices aim to integrate seamlessly into daily life, with the Humane Pin aspiring to replace smartphones altogether by projecting information and interactions onto the physical world. Conversely, the Rabbit R1 positions itself as a complementary tool, a "pocket companion" augmenting smartphone capabilities with its conversational interface and task-oriented approach. 
Despite their shared goal of offering hands-free assistance, the devices diverge in their marketed roles. The Humane AI Pin, with its ambition to be a "second brain" and "personal team," promises a holistic AI experience encompassing scheduling, communication, and even wellness coaching \cite{humane_home}. This positions the Humane Pin as a comprehensive life manager, anticipating needs and providing timely information through its various personality profiles. In contrast, the Rabbit R1 emphasizes task execution, envisioning a world where users command an "army of digital rabbits" to carry out specific actions \cite{rabbit_r1_launch}.  Rabbit’s technology is built on the premise of a  Large Action Model that is supposed to learn how to use any software it runs into, takes actions, and gets better over time by studying how people use online interfaces \cite{rabbit_research}. These distinctions highlight a key difference in their envisioned user relationships: the Humane Pin as a constant companion and the Rabbit R1 as a tool for delegated efficiency. 
While devices cast a wide net as general-purpose assistants, subscription services like Ohai and Docus adopt a tailored approach focusing on specific contexts and user needs. Ohai specializes in household assistance, particularly in managing schedules and  tracking to-dos through text and email interactions. The expressed purpose of Ohai is to \textit{‘lighten the mental load for everyone’} because managing a household and caring for loved ones is a significant contributor to burnout among Chief Household Officers."\footnote{Official website: \href{https://www.ohai.ai/about-us}{https://www.ohai.ai/about-us}, Instagram post: \href{https://www.instagram.com/ohaidotai/p/C198T-KplxZ/}{https://www.instagram.com/ohaidotai/p/C198T-KplxZ/}} This category of work includes organizing family calendars and sending timely reminders. Docus AI occupies the health and wellness niche, offering medical guidance, generating reports, and even providing second opinions. This targeted approach allows subscription services to leverage the power of GenAI models like OpenAI's GPT to deliver specialized assistance. The emergence of these two categories - devices and services - underscores the multifaceted nature of AI's integration into daily life. Devices offer the allure of constant, hands-free AI interaction, with ambitions ranging from task management to comprehensive life organization. Subscription services, on the other hand, often attempt to provide specialized expertise, addressing specific needs with tailored AI solutions.

%We intentionally included a diverse set of AI assistants over the legacy assistants precisely because their of their varied designs, intended purposes, and functionalities allowed us to comprehensively explore the wide spectrum of gratifications and uncertainties users encounter with emerging AI technologies. Rather than limiting our analysis to a single type of AI assistant, this diversity enables us to identify both unique and shared user experiences and perceptions across different interaction modalities. Consequently, our approach provides richer insights into the broader landscape of AI adoption and early adopters, clearly highlighting common user expectations and challenges while also identifying distinct gratification types and uncertainties relevant to different device categories.


\subsection{Data Collection and Analysis}
After receiving Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, over the course of 4 months, we conducted in-depth interviews with participants who purchased emerging AI devices and subscription services including Rabbit R1, Humane AI Pin, Docus and Ohai.All participants were required to show proof of purchase for devices and active subscription service status. Our semi-structured interviews lasted approximately 60 minutes and were conducted remotely by the first author. During our interviews we asked questions surrounding device expectations, motivations behind purchase, usage, and data privacy to understand if the promises purported by companies were realized in everyday use. Participants received compensation for their time in the amount of \$100 for successfully completing the interview. Participant backgrounds were diverse but gendered norms of early technology adoption were evident as shown in Table \ref{tab:demographics} below. We used a grounded approach to analyze all of our interview transcripts (n=9) \cite{charmaz2006constructing}. Applying practices of open coding and constant comparison to identify patterns and relationships in our data set. Initially a set of themes including minimizing distractions, personalization, distribution of labor, and mistake proofing  emerged from our findings. Refining themes continued to reveal disjunctions between use cases and privacy. These perspectives portrayed differing expectations of technology and assumptions about machine learning and artificial intelligence. The findings presented in this paper have the most insight to offer given the research question(s) focusing on understanding user motivations for adoption of emerging AI devices.

\section{Findings}
This section examines how participants made sense of and adapted to the capabilities and limitations of next-generation AI assistants. In \S\ref{sec:findings1_hype}, we explore how marketing-driven hype shaped user expectations and how those expectations clashed with the functional realities of devices like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin. In \S\ref{Comparisons to old}, we show how participants drew comparisons between legacy voice assistants and newer AI devices across functionality, content generation, and interaction modality. Building on this, \S\ref{sec:findings2_specific} highlights how users carved out value by integrating AI assistants into task-specific workflows or adopting domain-specific services like Ohai. Finally, \S\ref{sec:findings3_contradictions} explores contradictions in user expectations—particularly the tension between wanting proactive, emotionally responsive interactions and accepting the limited contextual memory and functional focus of current systems.

\subsection{Driven by Hype: Navigating Expectations versus Reality } \label{sec:findings1_hype}
Excitement and anticipation surrounding AI assistants like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin were intertwined with the aspirational promise of creating a "second version of the user" through technological advances like Large Action Models (LAM). By comparing marketing claims with the actual experiences of our participants, we highlight the gap between the proposed capabilities of these devices and their real-world performance. Understanding the perception and role of these technologies in our everyday lives also provides insight into how the public views AI which is necessary to develop trustworthy devices and tools. 

Participants in our study were drawn to purchase these devices and services due to their compelling advertising promising to streamline the mundane activities of a busy modern life. Best expressed by P2, a Rabbit R1 owner, \textit{"man, the advertisement, the YouTube videos, the Ted Talks, all that stuff was just like, whoa, really? That's crazy for \$199; you can't lose, you know what I'm saying?”} The utility of the device to record, memo, generate images and text summaries as well as offer seamless integration with services like Uber and Spotify, were all selling points. P4 thought the Rabbit would understand and execute commands with ease: \textit{"When I originally saw it, I thought it could have a very clear sense and just do it—like, have the ‘action’ part to it….like order me a pizza…and carry out the task…based on my past order(s).}\textit{” }Similarly, P3 purchased the Humane AI Pin based on \textit{“Ambient computing for the real world [was advertised]...and it looks sophisticated. You can also use it as it was shown (in the promos) and when I wear it I honestly feel it shows professionalism.”}

However, the discrepancy between the advertised ‘AI’ functionalities and the actual capabilities of these devices and services was particularly pronounced when they failed to execute tasks that were promoted as key capabilities. P2 expressed disappointment with Rabbit, stating, \textit{“When it was advertised, it indicated that it was a learning LAM, some type of learning module in which it would get the information and do all these tasks for you. It's not able to do that. That technology doesn't even exist."} 

One of the key features of Rabbit, as P2 explained, was \textit{"you're supposed to say, hey, get me an Uber to da da da da. Well, they can't do that because it depends on scripts, and if that website changes, those scripts no longer work."} P6 argued that these devices could not engage in dynamic interactions because they relied on rule-based static responses: \textit{"I will mess with [the Rabbit] logic, and it'll do the same thing…that's a pre-programmed response. I'll even say things like play me anything, excluding the Beatles, play me anything minus, Hey Jude, or play me anything that sounds kind of classic rock, and it'll still play the Beatles." }Despite the Rabbit R1’s claims of\textit{ intuitively learning}, P6 concluded that the device was only capable of so much: \textit{"I knew it was all marketing. I knew it was never going to be what they promised. I'm not fully disappointed.” }

While some participants were able to discern the lack of artificial intelligence, many conflated AI capabilities with more basic voice-activated commands. For example, P7 shared how awesome it was that the device would \textit{“connect me to the world without distracting me….I can just pick it up, push the button and say, what's the weather? Hey, when's the next basketball game?”} Limiting distractions through curated responses were common goals amongst participants. This mistaken understanding of AI leads to unrealistic expectations, diminished trust, and a lack of critical thinking about AI’s capabilities. This user mindset was described by P4, despite acknowledging its contributions where it did function well, concluded that the Rabbit is \textit{"a clicky [Mcdonalds] happy-meal toy [or] a Tamagotchi that speaks."} In fact, P4 thought there was so much of a gap between the promised functionality and the actual product that he was looking forward to joining \textit{“a class action lawsuit.”}

\subsubsection{Comparisons between Legacy Voice Assistants and Next-gen AI Assistants} \label{Comparisons to old}

This section explores how participants compared their experiences with traditional voice assistants (e.g., Amazon Alexa, Google Assistant) to next-generation AI assistants like the Rabbit R1 and Humane AI Pin. These comparisons centered around three key areas: (1) Functionality, (2) Content Creation, and (3) Modality.

\paragraph{Functionality:} Participants used legacy assistants for routine tasks such as smart home control (P5), reminders (P2), scheduling (P8), and shopping lists (P9). However, they noted limitations of legacy assistants in flexibility and conversational depth. P5 and P6 emphasized that AI assistants provided more elaborate responses, while P3 and P2 encountered inconsistent performance—such as failure to make a call, clunky media controls, and raw system messages instead of interpretable error messages—highlighting a lack of polish in newer systems compared to the error-handling finesse of Siri or Alexa.

\paragraph{Content Creation:} Legacy assistants were constrained to executing predefined commands and retrieving information from fixed or web-based sources. In contrast, participants like P1, P3, and P6 praised the Rabbit R1 for its generative capabilities, including the creation of novel content and handling of nuanced prompts. P2, for instance, used the Rabbit R1 to  generate visual content via Midjourney \cite{midjourney}, aiding in his social media campaign for mental health awareness.

\paragraph{Modality:} Participants also noted major differences in interaction design. The Rabbit R1, co-designed with Teenage Engineering \cite{teenage_engineering}, was described by P4 as “playful,” but its scroll wheel and non-touch interface frustrated users like P4 and P6, who expected touchscreen functionality. The AI Pin, with its gesture-based and screen-less interface, introduced a novel projection display. While P2 and P3 found it innovative—“beaming text onto your palm”—they also found it impractical in bright or uneven environments. P2 even returned the device, citing usability concerns.

In contrast, legacy assistants were embedded in familiar interfaces that required little adaptation. While some participants (P8, P9) appreciated the novelty of newer devices, others (P2, P4) preferred the intuitive and frictionless interactions offered by traditional systems.

\subsection{Beyond the Generalist: Adapting AI to Fit the User’s Ecosystem} \label{sec:findings2_specific}
Rather than expecting next-generation assistants to serve as general-purpose AI tools, participants who derived the most value identified specific use cases where these technologies integrated meaningfully into their broader technological ecosystems. This value was realized in two primary ways. First, participants adapted general-purpose devices like the Rabbit R1 to serve focused roles within customized workflows. By leveraging features such as voice recording or rapid information retrieval, they were able to offset the device’s broader limitations. Often, this involved integrating the assistant with other tools, positioning it as one part of a larger multi-device setup. Second, participants preferred services that were explicitly designed for specialized tasks, such as Ohai for calendar management or Docus for medical support. These purpose-built systems, typically powered by large language models trained on domain-specific datasets, offered tailored functionality that general-purpose assistants struggled to replicate. These examples of task-specific adoption show how users carved out productive roles for AI by aligning their strengths with real, contextual needs.

P6, a nurse with ADHD, created an intricate workflow that combined Rabbit and ChatGPT to reduce both time and cognitive effort during medical charting. As he explained, \textit{“The joke is that I have 30 seconds to [see the patient] and 30 minutes to chart it... Now I can do 12 [patients] within an hour… easily, easily!”} By uploading recordings from the Rabbit R1 into ChatGPT Plus, he generated summaries and detailed synopses for medical records, significantly streamlining his documentation process. He emphasized the cognitive relief this brought, particularly in light of his ADHD: \textit{“Even just the mental energy alone... is incredible.”} Though the Rabbit was marketed as a general-purpose device, it proved most useful when adapted to a specific, personalized workflow.

In contrast, services like Ohai were built with targeted functionality from the start. Ohai specializes in calendar management and was quickly embedded into participants’ daily routines. P1 described his typical use: \textit{“I just text: ‘I have a sales meeting tomorrow from 7 to 8:30 a.m....’ because I know Ohai can understand it and execute what I’m trying to get it to do.”} Participants appreciated how Ohai used natural language processing to interpret and act on input, distinguishing it from conventional digital calendars.

Both P1 and P2 preferred Ohai to general-purpose assistants like Gemini due to its task-specific precision and seamless integration across platforms. As P1 put it, \textit{“Ohai kind of bridges the gap between one of the purely generative AI models... and the integrations you would get with a workspace on Gemini.”} Ohai’s ability to connect both Google and Apple calendars also solved a long-standing issue for P1.

Importantly, P1 emphasized how Ohai recognized the complexity of his social roles—father, manager, son, caregiver—and adapted accordingly. Ohai helped him offload the cognitive burden of assigning tasks to appropriate social identities (e.g., caregiver vs. coworker) and prioritizing them based on context. P5, who lives with bipolar disorder, used Docus to reduce the cognitive strain of searching for medical information. Trained on a medical-specific corpus, Docus provided what he called a \textit{“50/50 success rate.”} He appreciated the system’s differential diagnosis feature, which mimicked doctor-patient conversations by adjusting responses as more symptoms were provided. However, he was frustrated when the system failed to answer a drug interaction query, instead recommending he consult a doctor. As he put it: \textit{“It’s not very useful if you ask the AI a question and end up getting recommended to consult your doctor again.”} Still, P5 remained optimistic, wishing the system were more proactive—even if it required disclaimers or additional data: \textit{“I’m not disappointed. But [I wish it were] more proactive.”}\footnote{Docus’s AI doctor feature offers connections with over 350 top doctors in the US and Europe for second opinions and expert validation.}

While these task-specific applications offered notable cognitive relief, P5’s experience underscores a key tension in user expectations: the desire for AI to be both conservative (e.g., not to give incorrect medical information) and proactive (e.g., provide medical answers based on user history). These contradictions in what users want from AI assistants are explored further in the next section.

\subsection{Designing for Utility and Empathy: What Users Want from AI} \label{sec:findings3_contradictions}

Providing functional support relies on a different set of capabilities than offering emotional or social support. As discussed in \S\ref{sec:findings1_hype}, marketing for next-gen AI assistants often promised functional benefits—efficiency, automation, and anticipatory task support. While our participants found value in these task-specific functions, many also hoped for emotionally intelligent interactions. They wanted assistants that reflected human-like mannerisms and could engage in socially appropriate, context-aware conversations. Yet, this desire for emotionally resonant, human-like behavior often conflicted with the current limitations in contextual memory and precision.

For example, although Docus could ask medically relevant questions, P5 was frustrated that it repeatedly requested information he had already provided. The assistant failed to retain prior context, making interactions feel disjointed. Similarly, Rabbit struggled with continuity. P4 noted, \textit{“If I say something in a conversation… and end it, the conversation is then gone.”} P6 echoed this sentiment: \textit{“I can’t tell it to remember things… Not really. Does it remember my preferences? No.”} As a result, P6 adapted his own communication style—\textit{“I convey my needs [to Rabbit] so much that now I do it with people too.”} The burden of remembering and repeating preferences shifted from the system to the user.

Despite these limitations, participants occasionally experienced moments of more engaging, human-like interaction. P4 described the Rabbit’s responses as conversational and responsive, stating it \textit{“feels like a conversation… it’ll ask you a question in the direction you’re thinking.”} P8 also praised the Rabbit’s ability to understand complex queries and return rich, narrated answers, distinguishing it from earlier assistants like Siri and Alexa. 

P9 described using Rabbit as a personal “biographer” during walks. They appreciated its conversational nature and the RabbitHole feature\footnote{\href{https://www.rabbit.tech/support/article/what-is-rabbithole}{https://www.rabbit.tech/support/article/what-is-rabbithole} — a secure cloud hub that logs past interactions, queries, and content.} that automatically generated a searchable journal: \textit{“If I want to go back again, I have the whole script of the conversation.”} P5 similarly hoped Docus would evolve from a task-based assistant into something more emotionally attuned. He imagined a future version that would feel like it cared about him: \textit{“It’ll know me so well that it'll say, ‘Hey, you haven’t spoken to your uncle in Cuba in a week. Want me to mark him on your calendar?’ I’d pay for that.”} Not all participants, however, wanted more emotional or proactive AI. P1 preferred Ohai over general-purpose assistants like Rabbit and Humane specifically because it stayed focused on functional support: \textit{“Organizing, organizing, organizing… work schedule, home schedule… no conflicts.”} While some users expressed concerns about AI gaining deeper access to their personal context, many were open to sharing data if it reduced cognitive load. P4 remarked: \textit{“I get the need for privacy… but I don’t care too much. Are you gonna give me more targeted ads? Cool, thank you.”} This reflects a transactional view of AI—where data sharing is an acceptable trade-off for convenience and personalization.

We explore the underlying themes that emerge from these juxtapositions between functionality and companionship, memory and interaction, control and convenience in the following sections.

\section{Discussion}
Our findings highlight a persistent gap between user expectations and the actual capabilities of AI personal assistants, revealing ongoing challenges in the adoption of emerging technologies. Users often encounter uncertainty about what these assistants can realistically do and how they fit into daily life, leading to mismatches between anticipated and experienced gratifications. These uncertainties—functional, interactional, and social—can erode trust, diminish user satisfaction, and limit long-term engagement. By mapping these uncertainties to distinct user gratifications, we identify strategies for better aligning expectations with system performance, grounded in the framework of Uses and Gratifications Theory.

As introduced in \S\ref{UGT}, UGT helps explain why users adopt new technologies and the extent to which these technologies fulfill specific needs—technological, utilitarian, hedonic, and social \cite{katz1973uses, rubin2009uses, lin2024unraveling}. While participants reported gratification in some interactions with AI assistants, others resulted in disappointment, revealing a disconnect between device functionality and user motivations. These mismatches generate uncertainty and interfere with the satisfaction of intended gratifications \cite{DalsgaardDindler, AckermanGap}. As noted in \S\ref{URT}, such uncertainties are central to understanding barriers in the adoption and continued use of AI systems.

While earlier work, including Lin and Ng \cite{lin2024unraveling}, examines gratifications and technology acceptance, it often overlooks how marketing hype shapes user expectations and how the failure to meet these promises fosters uncertainty. Our findings indicate that users approach AI assistants with complex, context-sensitive expectations—anticipating not just efficient task performance but also socially responsive, conversational experiences. When these expectations are unmet, particularly in areas like contextual memory and natural dialogue, users experience disappointment. Ackerman frames this disconnect as a “sociotechnical gap”: the divide between users’ socially situated needs (“social requirements”) and the limitations of technical implementation (“technical feasibility”) \cite{AckermanGap}. To explore how this gap plays out in everyday use, we introduce three forms of uncertainty—functional, interactional, and social—through the combined lenses of user gratification and mediated uncertainty \cite{zhang2022uncertainty, chang2024uncertainty}:

    \begin{enumerate} 
    \item \textbf{Functional uncertainty:} Users are unclear about the AI assistant’s actual capabilities and limitations, leading to confusion or hesitation in use. This uncertainty stems from ambiguous system boundaries, leaving users unsure of which tasks the assistant can reliably complete. This is detailed in \S\ref{sec:functional_uncertainty}.
    \item \textbf{Interactional uncertainty:} This refers to users’ uncertainty about how to effectively communicate with or issue commands to the assistant, often resulting in miscommunication, inefficient or frustrating interactions. This uncertainty is covered in \S\ref{sec:interaction_uncertainty}.
    \item \textbf{Social uncertainty:} Users express uncertainty about the assistant’s appropriate role in their social lives—whether it should act as a helpful tool, a social companion, or something in between. We explore this uncertainty in \S\ref{sec:social_uncertainty}.
\end{enumerate}

In this section, we map user gratifications and uncertainties to clarify the relationship between the types of gratification driving user adoption and different dimensions of technology uncertainties. For each of the uncertainties, we also provide design and policy recommendations that can alleviate the uncertainty. We summarize the relationships between these uncertainties and gratifications in Table \ref{tab:uncertainty_gratification}.

Our work further contextualizes recent literature on AI assistant particularly regarding how intent misalignment, tone mismatches, and perceived obstruction contribute to user uncertainty. As discussed in the new related work section, AI systems like ChatGPT frequently misinterpret user goals or overlook contextual cues, resulting in responses that feel irrelevant or out of step with user intent \cite{RAO2023990, kim_et_al_24}. These failures exacerbate interactional uncertainty, especially when compounded by tone mismatches, which can diminish users’ sense of being understood or respected during interactions \cite{RAY2023121}. Additionally, refusal to engage—particularly when prompted by controversial or sensitive topics—has been perceived as obstructive, even when framed in safety language \cite{borji2023categorical}. These patterns further illustrate how AI assistants fall short of social and hedonic gratifications, and they reinforce our framing of the sociotechnical gap: users expect contextually responsive, socially competent agents, yet current implementations often default to rigid, risk-averse responses that violate those expectations. These insights expand our categorization of functional, interactional, and social uncertainty by tying them directly to design failures in tone, intent recognition, and refusal logic, offering additional leverage points for both interface design and policy intervention which we present in the following sections.
